I am 63 years old and have been working these fields in Quzhou since I was a teenager. I never went to school, but I know this land. My family has about 7 mu of good flat land here on the North China Plain, and I do not rent extra land anymore — my back is not what it used to be.

The wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October after the autumn rains, the way my father taught me. I used the rotary tiller to prepare the soil after taking out the maize stalks, and I spread the compound fertilizer as basal dressing then. The wheat is sleeping through winter now, but when the Qingming season comes, I will irrigate it and top-dress with urea to make it strong. I will water it three or four times before harvest in early June, and spray for insects and diseases maybe three or four times — aphids and rust always come.

After we harvest the wheat in June, I will plant summer maize right away on the same 7 mu. I always buy hybrid maize seed from the supply shop now — the old saved seed cannot compete with the new hybrids like Denghai or Nongda, they grow faster and yield better. For maize, I do not till the soil again; we sow directly into the wheat stubble. This saves time, fuel, and my energy, and the stubble helps keep moisture. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat because the wheat left nutrients behind, but I still give it compound fertilizer at sowing and maybe one more top-dressing when it is knee-high. Two irrigations are usually enough for maize if the summer rain cooperates. I spray pesticides a few times too — especially when the borers start.

I do not grow cotton anymore. The labor is too much for an old man — all that pruning and spraying, and the prices jump around. Wheat and maize have steady buyers, and I can store some grain at home for my own flour and feed. My nephew helps me with the machine work now, and the rest I do myself.
